results.title: AppBlock Has 15 Million Users. Here’s What Its Own Reviews Reveal About Why It Doesn’t Work.
results.content:
### The Review That Says It All

One user reviewing AppBlock described exactly the moment that mattered most: they downloaded it expecting it to block their apps for a set period with no way to stop it early. Instead, they found they could disable the blocker at any moment they wanted. Their conclusion was blunt: that single feature made the entire app, in their words, “absolutely useless,” because if all that’s stopping you from reopening the apps is your own willpower, you never needed the blocker in the first place.

That’s not a minor complaint buried in a five-star sea of praise. That’s the exact core failure mode that makes most app blockers fail- a wall with a door built directly into it, available the moment your resistance is lowest. [...] ### The Honest Takeaway

Fifteen million downloads tell you AppBlock is popular. They don’t tell you it works for the person who needs it most. The most telling reviews on any app blocker’s page are rarely the five-star ones; they’re the honest, specific complaints from people who genuinely tried to fix something and found the exact loophole that let them fail again.

If you’ve read a review like that and thought “that’s exactly what happened to me,” the fix isn’t a better version of the same design. It’s a blocker built without the door in the first place.

I write about attention, focus, and honest comparisons of what actually works. I built Detach: a free iPhone app blocker at getdetach.app. Follow me on Medium for more.

Iphone App Blocker [...] ### To Be Fair, AppBlock Does Some Things Well

This isn’t a case of a badly-built app. AppBlock offers genuinely useful features: location-aware blocking rules, multiple profiles for work, study, or sleep, PIN-protected settings, and message muting during focus sessions. For someone with mild, occasional distraction who mainly needs a gentle scheduling tool, it can work reasonably well.

The problem is specifically for the person this product is most heavily marketed toward: someone with a genuine compulsive habit, searching at 1 am for a way to stop opening the same app for the fifth time that hour. For that specific person, a blocker with a built-in disable button and documented ways to silently fail isn’t a minor inconvenience. It’s the entire reason the attempt doesn’t work.

results.title: Best App Blockers for Android (2026) – Habit Doom
results.content:
An app that has to ask Android not to kill it is not a lock. Neither approach prevents the app starting.

So an Android block is a cover, not a lock. The app is running underneath it.

There is no equivalent of Apple's ManagedSettings layer, which genuinely prevents launch and lets an iPhone block survive a force-quit. And there are two more failure points on Android: you can revoke the overlay permission in Settings, and battery optimisation can put a blocker to sleep in the background, at which point it silently stops enforcing. On Android, the last switch always belongs to whoever is holding the phone. [...] No, and you should be sceptical of any app that claims otherwise. Android app blocking depends on an Accessibility Service, which the device owner can disable in system Settings. This is a genuine architectural difference from iPhone, where Apple's ManagedSettings layer allows a block to survive a force-quit. On Android the realistic aim is enough friction to break an automatic habit, not an unbreakable wall. [...] Two caveats. It advertises "uninstall prevention" and says bypassing is impossible, which is a stronger claim than the platform supports. And Strict Mode has moved behind a paid tier: a June 2026 review complains that the app "started as a completely free focusing app" and now costs around $10 a month, with the developer replying to confirm that stronger blocking is now Pro.

ActionDash (~68,900 reviews) is StayFree's sibling, and installing it makes that obvious: identical "join 20 million people mastering screen time and email inbox habits" onboarding, and the same Inbox Cleaning feature.
